clinicalPearls: A collagen VI-related myopathy sitting at the milder end of a spectrum whose severe pole is Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy
Combines slowly progressive proximal weakness with the characteristic pattern of distal joint hyperlaxity alongside more proximal joint contractures
Contractures typically affect the long finger flexors, elbows and ankles, and finger flexion contractures are a useful diagnostic clue
Most commonly inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern from mutations in the COL6A1, COL6A2 or COL6A3 genes, with recessive cases also described
Skin changes such as follicular hyperkeratosis and abnormal, keloid-like or atrophic (cigarette-paper) scarring reflect the connective-tissue basis of the disorder
Onset ranges from childhood to adult life and progression is generally slow, with many patients remaining ambulant into later adulthood
Respiratory function can decline even while ambulation is preserved, so surveillance of nocturnal respiration is important
reference.pathophysiology: Bethlem myopathy is caused by mutations in one of the three genes encoding the alpha chains of collagen VI, a microfibrillar extracellular-matrix protein that forms a network in the interstitium around muscle fibres and connects the basement membrane to the surrounding connective tissue. Defective assembly or secretion of collagen VI disrupts this network, impairing the mechanical and signalling interactions between muscle fibres and their matrix and contributing to fibre dysfunction, abnormal mitochondrial regulation and apoptosis. Because collagen VI is also important in tendon, skin and joint connective tissue, the disorder produces the combination of muscle weakness, the distinctive laxity-and-contracture joint phenotype, and characteristic skin abnormalities.
additionalInvestigations: Serum creatine kinase, which is usually normal or mildly elevated
Muscle magnetic resonance imaging showing a characteristic pattern of fatty change, including rim involvement of thigh muscles
Muscle biopsy with collagen VI immunohistochemistry, sometimes on cultured fibroblasts
Targeted genetic testing of COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3
Respiratory function tests including overnight monitoring for nocturnal hypoventilation
Assessment of joint contractures and skin findings
redFlags: Nocturnal hypoventilation or declining respiratory function despite preserved walking
Loss of independent ambulation requiring rehabilitation input
Features suggesting the more severe Ullrich end of the spectrum in a child
reference.prognosis: Bethlem myopathy is slowly progressive and most patients retain independent ambulation well into adult life, though a minority require walking aids later and respiratory involvement can develop, so lifespan is usually near normal with appropriate surveillance.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnostic combination of distal hyperlaxity with proximal contractures
Failing to monitor respiratory function because ambulation is preserved
Missing the connective-tissue skin clues that point to collagen VI disease
Assuming normal collagen VI immunostaining excludes the diagnosis, as it can be normal or only subtly abnormal in milder cases
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy; physiotherapy and regular stretching to preserve range of movement and limit finger-flexor, elbow and ankle contractures
Occupational therapy, orthoses and splinting, and mobility aids to maintain function and ambulation
Orthopaedic referral for surgical release of disabling contractures
Respiratory surveillance with spirometry and overnight monitoring for nocturnal hypoventilation, introducing non-invasive ventilation when it develops
Attentive skin and wound care given the tendency to abnormal keloid-like or atrophic scarring
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular team follow-up coordinating neurology, respiratory and rehabilitation care
Genetic counselling for the collagen VI (COL6A1, COL6A2, COL6A3) inheritance, usually autosomal dominant but sometimes recessive
